input: In this worked example, the goal is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and, in addition, to determine the fraction of the reactant that remains after 60 min have elapsed. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) fixes the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by the relation $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after a time $t$ (min) is given by $\exp(-k t)$. In the case considered here, the measured rate constant is $k$ = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, a value obtained from concentration measurements that were taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min. When the relevant substitutions are carried out, the worked results are a half-life of 10 min and a fraction remaining after 60 min of 0.02 (dimensionless), both of which are computed from the relations stated above. It is important to note that these relations are valid only for a first-order reaction, and a reaction of another order would follow a different decay law, so the results obtained here cannot simply be transferred to reactions that do not exhibit first-order behaviour. The concentration measurements on which the value rests were taken at regular intervals across the stated period, and because the temperature was held at 323 K throughout the measurements, the value of $k$ obtained applies to that temperature and to no other. The half-life has the further convenient property that it does not depend on how much reactant is present at the start, and it is precisely this independence that marks the first-order case out from the behaviour shown by reactions of other orders, where the corresponding time changes with the starting concentration. Overall, the example demonstrates how a single measured rate constant, namely $k$ = 0.069 min-1, is sufficient to determine both the half-life of 10 min and the fraction remaining after the stated time interval.
target: Compute the half-life of a first-order reaction with rate constant $k$ = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) fixes the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after time $t$ (min) is $\exp(-k t)$. The rate constant was obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. Substitution of $k$ = 0.069 min-1 in the half-life relation gives a half-life of 10 min. Substitution of the same value in the decay relation at $t$ = 60 min gives a fraction remaining of 0.02, dimensionless. The two results are consistent with each other: the decay relation returns the half value at a time equal to the half-life, and the stated results satisfy that check at 10 min. The concentration measurements follow the decay across several half-lives, so the rate constant rests on the shape of the whole decay and not on a pair of endpoints read at the start and the end. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither result carries over to such a reaction: the half-life would then depend on the starting concentration, and the fraction remaining would follow the decay law of that order instead. The worked results therefore rest on the order being established before the relations are used. The measured value of $k$ also belongs to 323 K. At another temperature the rate constant changes, and the half-life and the fraction remaining change with it, so both results are quoted at the temperature of the measurement and at no other. Both results are read as properties of the reaction at the stated temperature, obtained from the stated measurements, and neither result extends to a reaction whose order has not been established or to a temperature at which $k$ has not been measured.
